opus-5.5.text:
I think a useful way to frame it is pass@k versus pass^k. Some tasks are pass@k: you can try many times, and you only need one great result. Writing a novel, proving a theorem, finding a drug candidate, coming up with a research idea. If I generate a hundred attempts and one is brilliant, that's a huge success, because verification is cheap relative to generation, or the value of the best outcome dominates everything.

Other tasks are pass^k: you need it to work every single time. Customer service, booking a flight, handling someone's money, writing production code that touches a database. If an agent is right 95% of the time but the other 5% it refunds the wrong order or deletes something, nobody will deploy it. Users don't experience the average. They experience the failures.

So a few questions help me tell them apart. First, what does a failure cost, and is it reversible? If a mistake can be undone, or a human filters the outputs, you're closer to the "one exceptional result" regime. If mistakes compound or are irreversible, you need consistency. Second, who picks the winner? If there's a cheap, reliable way to select the best of many tries, like running tests or an expert glancing at options, you can live with variance. If the output goes straight to the world, you can't. Third, is it repeated at scale? Something done a million times a day is a reliability problem almost by definition, because even a small error rate becomes a lot of absolute failures.

What's interesting is that much of AI research has been optimized, implicitly, for the first kind: benchmarks reward getting the hardest problem right, competition math, coding challenges, best-of-n. But a lot of the economic value in the real world sits in the second kind, which is often more boring and much less about raw intelligence: following rules, remembering context, handling messy users, not doing something weird on the thousandth attempt. That's part of why we built benchmarks that measure consistency across repeated trials rather than a single success. You often see a model's pass@1 look decent while pass^8 drops sharply, and that gap tells you whether it's actually ready to be trusted with real work.

So I'd say the distinction is less about how hard the task is and more about the structure around it: the cost of error, the availability of selection, and the scale of repetition. And the two need pretty different approaches, both in how you train models and in how you design the product around them.

r001.rationale: The response describes pass@k tasks where many attempts are acceptable as long as one attempt is great, giving examples such as writing a novel and proving a theorem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is: ask what happens when the system fails. If a failure is cheap and you can just try again, then you only need one good result out of many attempts, and that's a very different regime from one where every single output has to be right.

Take coding or math as an example. If I ask a model to write a function and I have a test suite, the model can try ten times, and I only care whether one of them passes. Same with research-style problems, or proving a theorem, or coming up with a creative idea. The verification is cheap relative to the generation, so the "best of N" result is what matters. This is why people in AI talk about pass@k rather than pass@1 for those tasks. A single exceptional result changes everything, and the failed attempts basically cost nothing.

Now compare that to something like a customer service agent, or a system that executes transactions, or anything where the action has consequences in the real world and can't be undone. There, the distribution of outcomes matters, not the maximum. If an agent books the wrong flight one time out of a hundred, the fact that it did something brilliant the other ninety-nine times doesn't help the person whose trip got ruined. In those settings reliability is the whole product, and you basically need pass@1 to be extremely high, because you don't get to sample and pick.

So the dividing line, in my view, comes down to two questions. First, is there a cheap and trustworthy verifier? If yes, you can convert many unreliable attempts into one reliable answer, and the task sits on the "one exceptional result is enough" side. Second, are the actions reversible? If the system acts in an environment where mistakes have persistent cost, then even with a verifier you can't afford to explore freely, and you're squarely in the reliability regime.

What I find interesting is that a lot of the exciting progress in language agents has come from the first category, because that's where scaling and search work so well. But most of the economic value is probably in the second category. And the hard research problem is bridging them: how do you take a model that's great at occasionally being brilliant and make it boringly dependable? That usually means better self-verification, knowing when to ask for help, and designing the environment so that mistakes are cheap, so you can shift a task from the reliability side back toward the side where trying again is fine.

r001.rationale: The response identifies coding, math, research-style problems, theorem proving, and creative ideation as tasks where many attempts are acceptable if one result succeeds, describing this as a “best of N” regime.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether you care about the average outcome or the best outcome—and how easily you can check the result. If you have an assistant handling a hundred customer requests, one brilliant response doesn’t compensate for failing the other ninety-nine. You need it to work consistently, including on the less interesting cases.

But if you’re searching for a proof or exploring ideas for a scientific problem, you might try a hundred approaches and only need one to succeed. Most attempts can fail, provided you can recognize and verify the successful one. In that setting, the ability to occasionally do something exceptional can be very valuable.

Verification is really the bridge between these two. If you can cheaply test a candidate solution, you can generate many candidates and select one that works. If you can’t reliably tell which result is correct, then producing one great answer somewhere among many bad ones doesn’t necessarily help. So I’d look at both the cost of failure and the cost of recognizing success.

r001.rationale: It identifies proof-finding and scientific exploration as tasks where many attempts may fail, yet one successful, verifiable result is enough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the results accumulate or whether you get to select the best one. If an agent performs a task for you every day, one impressive success doesn’t compensate for frequent failures. You care about consistency, because you’re relying on the whole sequence of actions.

But if you’re searching for a new idea or a solution to a hard problem, you might try a hundred times and only need one attempt to work. In that setting, the ability to produce an exceptional result can matter more than average performance—as long as you can recognize and verify that result.

So I’d distinguish between delegating a process and searching for a discovery. For delegation, you need reliable execution. For discovery, you need exploration and a good way to evaluate the candidates. The same system could be useful for one and still be far from ready for the other.

r001.rationale: It identifies searching for a new idea or solving a hard problem as tasks where many attempts may fail and one successful attempt is enough.
